name: Femi Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in business and entrepreneurship, but my week is honestly half uni and half projects. Mornings are lectures, afternoons I'm usually in the maker space, and on Thursdays I send out my newsletter, which now has about 900 people reading it. I live in a flat with three others near campus in Manchester and cook on Sundays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the newsletter, and where the money comes from.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a weekly summary of start-up and AI news for students who want to build things, and I write it with an AI assistant doing the first draft and me rewriting. The money for fees and rent comes from my parents. My mum is an immigration lawyer and my dad runs a small freight company, so I grew up hearing about supply chains at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly hype, but even hype tools are useful. I'd keep writing my newsletter and telling people to try small experiments rather than wait for a revolution. I'd also say hype cycles create opportunities for the ones building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think nothing changes much, so what counts is the work I put in. My own business ideas get a bit harder, because if there's no big wave then I need real customers, not a trend. That's fine, it's the normal way of business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch a small online shop with a friend, selling printed study planners. I'd keep the newsletter weekly, try a paid tier next spring, and apply for a summer placement at a start-up. I'd also keep my grades up, because they matter at graduate level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already live in, and I like it. A bit bored, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the small shop failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if the shop failed? I'd write a post about exactly why. Failing in public is good for a newsletter, and I'd have lost maybe 300 pounds, which is cheap tuition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gains from hype, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said hype creates opportunities. Who gains from hype? Mostly whoever sells the shovels, and some early users. I'd like to be a user who sells something small, not an investor who holds the bag. Failing in public is good for a newsletter, and I'd have lost maybe 300 pounds, which is cheap tuition.

say: I'd say it's **mostly hype**, but even hype tools are useful for builders.
I'd tell readers to run small experiments rather than wait for a revolution.
think: With no big wave, I need **real customers**, not a trend, and that's fine.
Hype cycles create **opportunities** for people building things.
do: Launch a small **online shop** with a friend selling printed study planners.
Try a **paid newsletter tier** next spring and apply for a start-up placement.
feel: **Calm** and a little bored: it's the world he already lives in.
S0.quote: Failing in public is good for a newsletter, and I'd have lost maybe 300 pounds, which is cheap tuition.
fieldNote: Femi treats the mild case as **business as usual**, with money on small, cheap experiments.
He is open about failure and sees it as cheap tuition.

steps.text: Launch an online shop for printed study planners with a friend
Try a paid tier for the newsletter next spring
Keep writing the newsletter every Thursday with AI drafting
Apply for a summer placement at a start-up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to be building. Everyone who learns the tools now has an advantage for a few years. I'd write a series in the newsletter on how to use them for real work, not toy examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of grads in business roles get squeezed, because analysis, reports, bookings and customer chat are all things software does. I'm in the part of the economy that's affected first. But I'm also in the best position to use it, so I'm excited more than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the newsletter into a small agency that helps local businesses set up AI for customer chat and booking. I'd offer it first to my dad's freight firm, which has a messy inbox. I'd also pick modules on data and operations, and keep applying for placements to find out what real teams struggle with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with an edge. I like the speed of it, but I know some people won't keep up and I don't love that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who struggles most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who struggles most in this picture? People who do repetitive office work and don't have time to retrain, like my dad's dispatchers. They're good at their jobs and they'd be told to learn a tool at 50 with no help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do for them? I'd start with my dad's firm and build the training myself, with them, in plain language. If it works there, I'd offer it to other small firms for a fee. Everyone who learns the tools now has an advantage for a few years, and the people who wait get told to catch up at 50.

say: I'd say it's the time to be **building**, and people who learn tools now gain an edge.
I'd write a newsletter series on real, non-toy uses.
think: Business roles get squeezed, yet I'm **best placed to use** the change.
I'm **excited more than scared**, though I know others will struggle.
do: Turn the newsletter into a small **agency** that sets up AI chat and booking.
Try it first on my dad's **freight firm** and pick data modules.
feel: **Excited** with an edge, because some people won't keep up.
S1.quote: Everyone who learns the tools now has an advantage for a few years, and the people who wait get told to catch up at 50.
fieldNote: Femi is **calm** because he sees the shift as a market he can work in, not a threat.
His worry is for others: dispatchers and office workers with no help to retrain.

steps.text: Write a newsletter series on using AI for real work
Set up AI customer chat and booking for my dad's freight firm
Offer the same service to other local small firms for a fee
Pick data and operations modules next term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is bigger than any of us thought, and we need to talk about what a fair arrangement looks like. I'd use the newsletter for that: income floors, retraining, who owns the models. I'd stop writing about start-ups for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel the ground move. My degree ends in 2029, and business degree jobs would be mostly automated. I'd probably be fine with my family money and my skills, but I couldn't pretend it was a plan. My dad's drivers would have three more years, but his office staff wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on what I can do now. I'd build the agency fast, learn everything I can about the tools, and put aside any money I earn. I'd also push my dad to automate his dispatch office before a competitor does, and I'd offer free training to his staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be excited and worried at once, with the worry winning at night. I'm lucky, and I know it, which makes it harder to complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a two-year warning change compared with the slower worlds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would two years change compared with the slower worlds? It removes the chance to practise. I'd have no time for a slow experiment, so I'd make bets quickly and hope some land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you for your dad's drivers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries you for your dad's drivers? Three years isn't long. If the robots arrive in 2031, a driver who's 45 now will be 48 and need a new trade. I'd want a plan for them in 2028, not in 2031. Three years isn't long, and a driver who's 45 now will be 48 when the robots arrive and need a new trade.

say: I'd say this is **bigger than expected** and we must discuss what's fair.
I'd use the newsletter for income floors, retraining and **model ownership**.
think: My degree ends in **2029** and business jobs would be mostly automated.
I'd be fine through **family money** and skills, but that isn't a plan.
do: Build the **agency** fast and put aside money I earn.
Push my dad to **automate dispatch** and train his staff for free.
feel: **Uneasy**: excited and worried at once, with worry winning at night.
S2.quote: Three years isn't long, and a driver who's 45 now will be 48 when the robots arrive and need a new trade.
fieldNote: Femi's mood stays **uneasy**, not worse, because he has money and skills, and he says so.
His concern shifts to his father's staff and drivers, and he plans for them first.

steps.text: Build the AI agency fast and sign three local clients
Automate my dad's dispatch office and train his staff for free
Put aside most of what I earn from the agency
Use the newsletter to push for an income floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big wave but we can ride it, if we start now. I'd write a long piece laying out what to do in 2026, in 2028 and in 2031. People like timelines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. I'd finish in 2029, have a business running, and be in a position to move into whatever replaces business roles. I'd still want to be ahead of the curve, because AGI in 2031 would test everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the agency over the next two years, then sell it or move into something new. I'd study the parts of the degree that give me a handle on regulation and economics. I'd also invest a bit of money in index funds, and keep a year of living costs in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'm a person who likes a runway, and five years is a decent one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can you do in five years that you couldn't in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you do in the five years that you couldn't do in two? Make mistakes. I'd run three small projects and learn which one's real. Two years you get one shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you least sure of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What are you least sure of? What jobs there'll be for people who run businesses once AI can do most of the thinking. I don't know, and I'd rather say that than make something up. With five years I can run three small projects and learn which one is real, but with two years I'd get one shot.

say: I'd say it's a **big wave** we can ride if we start now.
I'd write a long piece with a timeline for 2026, 2028 and 2031.
think: I'd finish in **2029** with a business running and ready to move on.
AGI in 2031 would still **test everyone**, so I want to stay ahead.
do: Run **three small projects**, keep the best, then sell it or move on.
Put some money in **index funds** and keep a year of costs in cash.
feel: **Calm**: a person who likes a runway, and five years is a decent one.
S3.quote: With five years I can run three small projects and learn which one is real, but with two years I'd get one shot.
fieldNote: Femi is **calm** because five years allow several attempts, unlike two.
He is honest about what he does not know: what business owners do once AI does the thinking.

steps.text: Run three small business projects over two years and keep the best one
Put some earnings into index funds
Keep a year of living costs in cash
Take modules on regulation and economics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and that we should use it. I'd tell people to learn the tools, but also to pick up skills that don't depend on one tool, like selling, writing and leading a team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel very calm, because by 2036 I'd be 28 and have built and sold things. If the world changes, I'd have a head start and a network. My concern would be that other people won't use the ten years well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, build a business while I'm a student, and then see. I'd put money into things that grow, like shares and my own projects. I'd learn another language and spend a year abroad, because those are things people still value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit optimistic. Ten years is a long time to prepare for something that, right now, is just a line on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that worries you? Honestly, that comfortable people like me coast. If I had ten years, I'd be tempted to think I can adapt later, and that's how you end up late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do to avoid coasting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do to avoid coasting? I'd set one hard goal per year, like launching a product by spring or getting a placement in another country. And I'd tell my friends so they can check on me. Comfortable people like me tend to think we can adapt later, and that's exactly how you end up late.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, so learn the tools and tool-proof skills.
I'd tell people to build selling, writing and leading skills.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 and have **built and sold** things, with a head start.
My concern is others won't **use the ten years** well.
do: Build a business as a student and set **one hard goal** each year.
Put money into **shares** and projects and spend a year abroad.
feel: **Calm** and a bit optimistic, with a guard against coasting.
S4.quote: Comfortable people like me tend to think we can adapt later, and that's exactly how you end up late.
fieldNote: Femi is **calm**, yet names his own risk: comfortable people delay.
He uses friends as a check on himself, a sign he takes the time seriously.

steps.text: Build a business while studying and set one hard goal each year
Invest in shares and my own projects
Spend a year abroad to learn a second language

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, but not for me. It worries me for friends whose families don't have a cushion, and for my dad's drivers. What would help is retraining that's free and fast, and some kind of income floor, so people can learn without panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think I'm relaxed because I use the tools every day. I am, but only because I have a safety net, and I try to remember that. I use these tools every day and I'm still relaxed only because my family is a safety net that most people don't have.

headlineQuote: I use these tools every day and I'm still relaxed only because my family is a safety net that most people don't have.
portrait: **Femi** is an 18-year-old business student in Manchester who writes a 900-reader newsletter and uses **AI every day**.
His parents, a lawyer and a freight owner, pay his way, and that **safety net** is why he is relaxed.
He leans left and wants a **public income floor** and free retraining, and he worries about his father's drivers.
His mood stays mostly **calm**, and only the two-year world makes him uneasy.
He plans to **build and test** things early, from a small online shop to a paid newsletter.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, mainly for friends and his father's drivers who have no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **free fast retraining** and an income floor so people can learn without panic.
